content: Healthcare should be free from preventable infections, as no one should become ill while seeking medical care. However, globally, hundreds of millions of people are affected annually by healthcare-associated infections (HAIs), many of which are entirely avoidable. No healthcare system, regardless of its sophistication or development, is immune to HAIs. Infection prevention and control (IPC) play a critical role in addressing this issue. Preventing HAIs is more important than ever. IPC is a practical, evidence-based approach designed to protect both patients and healthcare workers from harm caused by preventable infections. Effective IPC requires consistent action at all levels of the healthcare system, from policymakers to facility managers, healthcare workers, and patients. HAIs are infections acquired during care delivery in healthcare facilities that were not present or incubating at the time of admission. These infections can also affect visitors, family members, and healthcare workers. Most HAIs are caused by microorganisms resistant to commonly used antibiotics, with common examples including urinary tract infections, chest infections, bloodstream infections, and wound infections. Several factors contribute to HAIs. In all settings, these include inappropriate use of invasive devices and antibiotics, high-risk diagnostic or therapeutic procedures, immunosuppression, severe underlying illnesses, and inadequate application of IPC precautions. HAIs are a significant public health issue, often gaining attention only during outbreaks or epidemics, such as the Ebola virus outbreak in West Africa. HAIs cause unnecessary deaths, impose a human and economic burden, prolong hospital stays, create long-term disabilities, and contribute to the growing problem of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Without regular HAI surveillance as part of an IPC program, it is impossible to recognize the local and national burden of HAIs and prioritize actions effectively. Globally, approximately 1 in 10 patients is affected by HAIs. In acute care hospitals, 7 out of every 100 patients in developed countries and 15 out of every 100 in developing countries acquire at least one HAI. In intensive care units, up to 30% of patients in high-income countries and 2–3 times more in developing countries are affected by HAIs. Unsafe injection practices are also a concern, with up to 70% of injections in some developing countries administered using reused syringes and needles. Additionally, 61% of healthcare workers globally do not adhere to recommended hand hygiene practices. In neonatal care, infections account for 4–56% of all neonatal deaths among hospital-born babies. In maternal care, up to 20% of women in Africa develop wound infections after cesarean sections, impacting their health and ability to care for their newborns. Patients infected with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) are 50% more likely to die than those infected with non-resistant strains. Effective IPC programs can significantly reduce HAI rates. In England, MRSA rates declined by 56% over four years, while in Africa, a safety culture and prevention program reduced surgical site infection risk by 44%. Australia achieved and sustained 80% hand hygiene compliance nationwide between 2010 and 2015. The World Health Organization (WHO) has been instrumental in advancing IPC globally. Its Clean Care is Safer Care program, launched in 2005, has provided technical support and leadership to strengthen IPC efforts worldwide. The SAVE LIVES: Clean Your Hands campaign, launched in 2009, has redefined hand hygiene advocacy, achieving widespread support and behavioral change. Over 50 countries have delivered national hand hygiene campaigns, and more than 30 countries have implemented local production of alcohol-based hand rubs using WHO guidance. WHO’s IPC Global Unit continues to lead efforts to strengthen national and international IPC capacity, improve practices, and change behaviors to make healthcare safer and free from avoidable infections. Their work supports WHO’s six core functions: leadership, research, monitoring, setting norms and standards, providing policy options, and offering technical support. To succeed in IPC, WHO is developing new policies, evidence-based recommendations, and tools to support governance, knowledge improvement, and implementation at the point of care. For example, the development of surgical site infection prevention guidelines demonstrates this commitment. Looking ahead, mobilizing resources and supporting the development of action and implementation plans will remain a key focus. The vision of WHO’s IPC efforts is to protect the lives of patients and healthcare workers worldwide through excellence in IPC. The mission is to elevate IPC to the top of national health agendas by providing innovative, effective technical guidelines and strong coordination, with the ultimate goal of reducing infections and AMR in healthcare settings.
